turns.speaker: A
turns.text: In watchmaking, any function beyond showing the hours, minutes and seconds is called a complication. A date window is a simple complication. So is a second time zone, a moon phase display or a chronograph, which works like a stopwatch.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Some complications are far more difficult than others. One example is the perpetual calendar. A normal date display needs to be corrected at the end of short months. A perpetual calendar knows how many days each month has, and even accounts for leap years. If it keeps running, it can show the correct date for decades without adjustment.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Another famous complication is the minute repeater. When you press a button, small hammers strike tiny gongs inside the case and ring out the time. It was originally made so people could know the time in the dark.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So what is a Grand Complication? There is no single official rule, but traditionally it describes a watch that combines several major complications in one movement. Often, it includes a striking function like a minute repeater, an astronomical function like a perpetual calendar, and a timing function like a chronograph.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Building such a watch takes great skill and many months of work. The parts must fit into a small case and work together without problems. That is why Grand Complications are among the most valuable watches in the world.
